The eleven ratings for Judges Scientific
Judges Scientific plc (JDG-GB) · Investment memo

Judges Scientific: orders have turned, the market has not priced the operating leverage, and the 22 January 2027 trading update decides the case

25 October 2026. Share price 3,425p (22 October 2026). Market capitalisation about £230m; enterprise value about £274m. All profit figures are on the company’s adjusted basis. Definitions and sources are in the end notes.

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in brief: Judges Scientific’s order intake has already recovered, but its revenue, its earnings and its share price have not, and the market has not priced how much profit the returning revenue will bring back.

Judges is a maker of niche scientific instruments with a cost base that is about half fixed, and it sits at trough earnings on a trough multiple. FY26 adjusted EPS of about 191p is 49% below FY23’s 375p. The shares trade at 12.3x two-year-forward earnings on the model’s EPS (14.5x on consensus), which is the 0th percentile of the stock’s five-year range and the 9th percentile of its ten-year range.

Order intake growth has recovered from −18% in Q1 2026 to about +15% in Q3 2026 (−1% for the year to late September), while FY26 revenue will fall about 14%. Roughly £20m of booked demand therefore sits between order intake and revenue, and that demand converts into revenue in Q4 2026 and H1 2027. On Judges’ half-fixed cost base, each £1 of regained revenue returns 40p to 45p of operating profit, whereas consensus forecasts embed only 18p to 24p.

The market already knows every negative: US research funding, China, the deferral of Geotek’s coring expedition, the CFO’s departure, 1.1x dividend cover, 2.1x leverage and three downgrades in three years. The market has not done the arithmetic of the positive, and that asymmetry is the investment case. The price of entry is exposure to one quarter that nobody can observe in advance: Q4 2026 shipments, which the company reports on about 22 January 2027.

The seven insights that matter

1
The gap between orders and revenue is the most under-reported fact about Judges. FY26 order intake will finish within a few per cent of FY25, while FY26 revenue falls 14%. Because revenue follows order intake by about four months, most of the model’s H1 2027 revenue growth of +13% is already in the order book. No broker or commentator states this, and the gap between orders and revenue is the mechanical foundation of the model’s FY27 EPS of 234p, against 219p in consensus.
2
Every broker describes Judges’ operating leverage, but no broker’s model captures it. Consensus FY27 EBIT of £22.0m on £128m of revenue implies an incremental margin of about 24%, which would require the company to add about £3m of cost on £7m of extra revenue. The model’s realised incremental margin is 42%: a 65% gross contribution, less returning semi-variable costs and wage inflation net of price increases. The difference between a 24% and a 42% incremental margin is worth about 17p of FY27 EPS on its own. Shore Capital also uses a 23% tax rate against the 18% to 21% that the company guides and that recurs, so the latent upgrade to the lowest broker forecast is about 25p.
3
The next trading update is the main risk, and the market already half expects a shortfall. The model’s FY26 EPS of 191p is 4% below the 199p consensus. The probability-weighted figure is about 188p, with a one-in-three chance of 165p to 185p. In both of the last two years in which earnings were weighted to Q4, the January update fell short of September’s expectations, and management has already signalled a heavier-than-usual Q4 and customers’ requests to defer shipments. The shares fell 20% after a results update that held guidance, so a January update that is “slightly below” is partly priced; a Q4 revenue slip of more than about £5m is not.
4
The out-year earnings come in two layers, and the model’s +102% return needs both layers. Organic-only EPS rises from 191p in FY26 to 292p in FY29 and 320p in FY30. The base case adds acquisitions from H2 2027 (about £47m deployed at 5.5x EBIT) and one Geotek coring expedition in FY29, which together lift FY29 EPS to 393p. The model’s 18-month total return of +102% applies the 17.05x guideline multiple to that 393p; the same multiple on organic FY29 EPS of 292p gives about +52%. Both returns are large against a 3,425p share price. Richard should hold the organic return as the base case and treat the acquisition and coring layers as options with dates attached.
5
The recovery is cyclical and runs at half the old compounding speed; it is not a return to the founder-era record. The dividend, growing 10% a year, absorbs 70% to 78% of free cash flow through FY28. Net debt to EBITDA therefore falls only slowly (1.7x at end-FY26, 1.5x at end-FY27), and acquisitions can be funded with debt only as EBITDA grows. About £6m of structural cost added since FY23 (the central team, UK tax and National Insurance changes, and R&D) caps the operating margin at recovered volumes at about 20%, against 26% at the FY22 to FY23 peak. The company’s ambition of a 30% return on total invested capital (ROTIC) is out of reach in the window: the model has about 12% in FY26 and 15% in FY28.
6
Sterling is the largest single sensitivity, and nobody has quantified it. About 50% of Judges’ revenue is in US dollars and 33% in euros, against a cost base that is 80% to 90% in sterling and hedged for about twelve months. A sustained 10% appreciation of sterling against both currencies would cost £4m to £7m of operating profit, or 47p to 83p of EPS, with a lag of two to four quarters. No broker model includes this sensitivity, and neither does the model, which assumes sterling at $1.30 to $1.38.
7
Judges’ valuation multiple moves on company news, so the re-rating will come from Judges’ own reporting calendar. Over the last six months, Judges’ daily share price returns have shown no correlation with those of its sector peers (R-squared 0%; Judges −27.5%, the peer basket +7.5%). No semiconductor rally will lift the shares, and no sector sell-off need sink them. Three dated company events decide the case, and the timeline below gives my probabilities for each.

The skew. The risk-reward is skewed down for the next trading update and up for the four reports that follow. A 30% to 40% fall needs an earnings miss and a further de-rating together; a gain of about 50% needs only that booked orders ship, that operating leverage works on the way up as it did on the way down, and that the market pays a multiple at the 20th percentile of the stock’s own history. A known near-term risk in front of an unpriced mechanical recovery is the kind of setup Richard looks for. The setup is not yet confirmed: the trigger, the 22 January 2027 update, is dated but not yet observed.

The five judgements that move the value of the shares, with the arithmetic

The five judgements below decide most of the value of the shares, and each one comes with its sensitivity in pence of EPS. All sensitivities start from the model’s base case:

Base-case inputFY26FY27FY28
Revenue£125.2morganic growth of +£8.1morganic growth of +£7.3m
Adjusted EBIT£18.8m£22.6m£27.0m
Gross contribution on marginal revenue65%
Tax rate18%20%21%
Shares in issue6.70m6.75m6.80m

Judgement 1: Q4 2026 shipments convert, so H2 2026 revenue reaches £69.5m. Each £1m of Q4 revenue that slips into January 2027 removes £0.65m of EBIT (£0.53m after tax), or about 8p of FY26 EPS, and nothing else inside FY26 offsets the loss. A £3m slip takes FY26 EPS to about 167p, and a £5m slip takes it to about 151p. The analysts’ downside band of 165p to 180p assumes that some of the slipped revenue carries a low margin, and I use 165p to 175p as the realistic downside. After a slip, year-end adjusted net debt would be £44m to £46m (1.9x to 2.0x EBITDA) rather than £41m (1.7x).

Most of the slipped revenue would return in H1 2027 at the same contribution, adding back about 6p of FY27 EPS for each £1m shipped, but on this share’s history the price would fall 15% to 25% first. I put the probability of a slip of £3m or more at about one in three.

Judgement 2: the realised incremental margin is 42%, not the 24% that consensus implies. On FY27 organic revenue growth of £8.1m, a 42% incremental margin adds £3.4m of EBIT, consensus’s implied 24% adds £1.9m, and the full 65% contribution would add £4.9m. Each 10 points of incremental margin is worth £0.8m of EBIT, or about 9.6p of FY27 EPS; on FY28’s organic revenue growth of £7.3m, the same arithmetic gives about 8.5p per 10 points. FY27 EPS is therefore about 216p on consensus-type leverage, 234p on the model and about 251p if the company holds its costs flat.

What would hold the realised incremental margin below 40%
  • A recovery weighted to Materials Sciences, whose contribution margin is lower
  • Management rebuilding bonuses and R&D ahead of the margin recovery
  • A stronger pound
What would push it above 50%
  • The China refill, concentrated in high-margin vacuum and cryogenics products, dominating H1 2027
  • The underperforming businesses reaching break-even faster than the half-credit the model assumes

Judgement 3: organic revenue grows 6.5% in FY27, of which about 4 points is volume and 2.5 points is price. Each point of organic growth is about £1.25m of revenue, £0.8m of EBIT and 9.6p of EPS, so organic growth of +3% takes FY27 EPS to about 200p and +10% takes it to about 268p. Three components inside the 6.5% carry most of the risk:

  • The China refill. Deferred shipments of £4m to £6m are worth about 8p of EPS per £1m, so a refill of £2m instead of the £5m base costs about 23p.
  • US academic demand. US academic customers provide about 12% of revenue, so a second leg of funding cuts of 10% to 15% would cost £1.5m to £2.2m of revenue and 12p to 18p of EPS directly, or 20p to 30p including knock-on caution among other customers.
  • Europe. European orders fell 20% in H1 2026, and the base case already assumes a slow recovery.

Because only about 4 points of the 6.5% is volume, reported organic growth overstates volume growth: a reported organic figure of 5% in FY28 would mean volume growth of 2.5%, and a reported 2.5% would mean no volume growth at all.

Judgement 4: sterling stays between $1.30 and $1.38. A sustained 10% appreciation of sterling against both the dollar and the euro would remove £4m to £7m of operating profit before any repricing. The lower figure scales Oxford Instruments’ published sensitivity (£0.6m of profit per 1% move) to Judges’ size; the higher figure is the analysts’ estimate of Judges’ transaction exposure. The effect is 47p to 83p of EPS over a full year: 25p to 40p in FY27, because hedges cover the first half, and the full amount in FY28. A move to $1.40 (about 4.5%) would cost 21p to 37p a year. Repricing would recover perhaps a third of the loss within 12 to 18 months in commercial channels, and little in academic channels.

Judgement 5: the acquisition engine restarts in H2 2027, and one coring expedition sails in FY29. Each £10m deployed at 5.5x EBIT adds £1.8m of EBIT, or £1.2m after 6% interest on the debt that funds it: about 14p of EPS at full-year effect. The model’s deployment of £5m, £12m, £15m and £15m adds about 5p, 24p, 46p and 72p to EPS in FY27 to FY30. One coring expedition brings £7m of revenue at a 70% margin, worth about 55p of EPS in the year it sails. The analysts put the probabilities of the expedition at 25% for 2028, 35% for 2029, 20% for 2030 and 20% for no expedition inside the window. The four combinations of the two layers give the following FY29 outcomes:

FY29 combinationFY29 EPSPrice at the 17.05x guideline multipleTotal return to end-2027, with 229p of dividends
Organic only292pabout 4,980pabout +52%
Acquisitions, no coring338pabout 5,760pabout +75%
Coring, no acquisitions347pabout 5,920pabout +79%
Both layers (the model)393pabout 6,700pabout +102%

The judgement that moves the multiple: a clean January 2027 update would move the stock’s phase from “collapsing” to “turning up” and, because Judges’ multiple responds to company news, could lift the two-year-forward P/E from 12x to 15x and then to 17x within weeks. A Q4 revenue slip of more than about £5m would reset that sequence by six months and hold the multiple at 12x to 13x on reduced forecasts, a share price of about 2,600p to 2,900p.

1Tailwinds in the operating environment; absence of headwinds

The external environment is still a net headwind, but it has stopped worsening, and because four headwinds struck at once, a partial easing of any one of them has an outsized effect from the trough.

Evidence: the downturn. About two-thirds of Judges’ revenue follows public research budgets, and those budgets produced the worst run of demand in the group’s listed history. Group order intake fell 12% in H1 2026 (−18% in Q1, flat in Q2) as four headwinds struck together: US research funding, a change in Chinese import procedures, the deferral of Geotek’s coring expedition and weakness in Europe, with offshore wind postponements on top (detailed in the figure below). The commercial and industrial third of revenue (semiconductor, battery and Geotek services) grew, but it lifted only eight of the 25 businesses into growth.

Evidence: the stabilisation. The external forces have stopped worsening. Q3 2026 order intake rose about 15%, taking the year-to-date change from −12% to −1%, and the order book stood at 17.3 weeks of revenue in June 2026 (15.7 weeks in December 2025 and 17.4 weeks a year earlier). Funders and peers confirm the stabilisation: the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) spent its full $35.3bn extramural budget by 30 September 2026; Thermo Fisher’s academic and government revenue returned to low-single-digit growth; Bruker has reported four consecutive quarters of book-to-bill above 1.0; and both Judges’ management and JEOL say that the Chinese import procedure is being resolved.

Evidence: what still weighs. NIH cash outlays fell 9% in September and about 15% in the quarter. The US administration’s FY2027 budget request again proposes a cut to the NIH; the House of Representatives has countered with flat funding, and a stopgap funding bill runs to 11 December. Chinese distributors report customs clearance times of more than six months and some cancellations. Fugro’s offshore wind revenue fell 24%, and the EU’s 2028 to 2034 research framework tilts towards defence. The macroeconomic backdrop hurts the share more than the business: the US 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.1%, the market is not re-rating small, indebted UK stocks, and sterling stands at about $1.34.

Inference. The external picture is net negative but improving at the margin, and for the share the improvement matters more than the level. None of the forces has become a tailwind. The China catch-up is a refill of deferred orders rather than new demand; the US faces another stopgap funding year at best; and the semiconductor and AI capital spending that is lifting Renishaw (Q1 revenue +47%), Jenoptik and Oxford Instruments (orders +44%) reaches Judges only at the edges. What matters for the share is that three independent headwinds (US funding, China and coring) and one smaller headwind (offshore wind) struck at the same time, so a partial easing of any one of them has an outsized effect from a trough base. The asymmetry is therefore better than the level of the headwinds suggests.

So what. Treat FY26 as the trough. FY27 organic growth of 6% to 9% is mostly mechanical, because the H1 2026 comparison is weak (revenue −21%, EPS −72%) and Chinese deliveries deferred from 2026 will ship in 2027. Do not model a multi-year upswing, a return of US demand to its 2023 run-rate, or a coring expedition before 2028.

Strongest counter-case. Part of the decline was specific to Judges and will not return with research funding. Bruker and Oxford Instruments grew orders through the same US disruption, and Judges’ European weakness has no funding explanation. The analysts’ third research set puts £3m to £5m of the roughly £17m of lost organic volume in this company-specific category. FY27 revenue of £135m would still be £11m below FY25 and only £1m above FY23, so the rebound is a partial retracement. The model already allows for the company-specific loss, but Richard should not read “mechanical rebound” as “full recovery”.

What would change my view. Negatively: enacted US funding cuts of even half the budget request (US academic orders down a further 10% to 15%); Chinese customs clearance stretching into H2 2027 with cancellations rather than deferrals; or sterling above $1.40. Positively: US academic orders turning positive year on year at the July 2027 update.

Consensus versus my view. Consensus and the house brokers describe the headwinds accurately and assume a flat-to-slow recovery, which I share. My difference from consensus lies in the timing of revenue conversion (the gap between orders and revenue), not in the view of the environment.

Score: 34. The environment is still a net headwind for an exporter exposed to research funding and without an AI or data-centre business, but the environment has stopped deteriorating, and three independent negatives can ease at once from a trough.

2Internally-driven corporate change forces; absence of problems

The new team has built the right structure, but the structure adds little to earnings before FY28, the CFO is leaving, and the acquisition engine that made the company has not restarted.

Evidence: the transition. Judges is midway through a deliberate “Halma-isation”: a move to Halma’s model of autonomous subsidiaries overseen by a stronger central team. The founder, David Cicurel (chief executive from 2002 to 2026, holder of about 9.3% of the shares), became Non-Executive Chair in February 2026, and Dr Tim Prestidge (formerly of Renishaw and Halma, at Judges since 2023) became chief executive. The table lists the other changes.

AreaWhat the new team has changed
LeadershipA Group Acquisitions Executive (formerly in corporate development at Oxford Instruments), a Portfolio Chief Executive (formerly at Halma) and a Group Commercial Director (formerly at Oxford Instruments and Renishaw)
GovernanceAn Executive Committee, a Nomination Committee, a new Audit Committee chair, malus and clawback provisions, and a new auditor (RSM) after restatements prompted by the Financial Reporting Council
Cost and portfolioAbout £1.8m to £2.0m of annualised cost removed at underperforming businesses in H1 2026, with about £1.0m reinvested; Scientifica’s exit from multiphoton microscopy; Armfield’s insourcing of production
TargetsEach subsidiary asked for a three-to-five-year plan to double its EBIT
Commercial focusSubsidiaries’ selling effort pushed towards commercial and industrial markets, which management describes as “four to five times larger than academia”
Tax and financingEnhanced use of the Patent Box regime (adjusted tax rate of 18% in H1 2026 and guided for the year, against 23% in FY25); the bank facility extended to July 2030

The founder built the company through 25 acquisitions at about 6x EBITA, with an average ROTIC of 29%. The new team has completed no acquisitions in 21 months.

The problems: people. The transition coincides with the deepest downturn on record and has exposed real problems. The CFO, in post since 2015, the architect of Judges’ cash discipline and its main investor contact, resigned in September 2026 and leaves in September 2027, with no successor named. Three of the top four executives have changed within 18 months.

The problems: returns and the weak businesses. ROTIC has fallen from 22.7% in 2023 to 12.9% in H1 2026. Three businesses show the cost of the hands-off model: Armfield (goodwill fully impaired; market share down from 40% to about 15% since 2016), Fire Testing Technology (an FY25 loss of £1.2m on £5.1m of revenue, while its R&D was cut) and Scientifica (impaired). Central costs rose about 75% in FY25. There is no portfolio pruning (the group has a zero-divestment policy) and no group software platform. Staff turnover is 19%, against a UK average of 15%.

The problems: rigid capital allocation. The interim dividend was raised 10% at 1.1x cover, a level the Chair himself called “clearly not sustainable”, and the board rejects share buybacks even at a five-year-low multiple.

Inference. The design of the change is right, but its timing is poor. Internal change lowers the risk of further surprises from inside the portfolio and adds perhaps 15p to 30p of EPS by FY28, from cost actions, the Patent Box and half of the planned repair of underperforming businesses. Internal change cannot drive the earnings path; external volume does that. The decisive internal unknown is whether the new deal team can buy businesses at about 5x EBIT without the founder, while private equity pays 10x to 12x EV/EBITDA for UK industrial businesses with more than £1m of EBITDA and Chinese buyers compete for the same assets. Evidence on the deal team’s ability will not arrive before H2 2027.

So what. Expect conservative first FY27 guidance in March 2027. The new chief executive’s bonus depends on budget EPS (it paid 5% of the maximum for 2025), and a departing CFO will want to hand over a clean floor. Do not credit acquisitions until a deal completes. The model includes acquisitions from H2 2027 at half the historical pace and identifies their contribution separately.

Strongest counter-case. The new intervention model is catch-up rather than best practice: ISO 9001 certification by 2027, monthly forecasting and internal audit are things Halma did twenty years ago. Layering Halma-trained central management on a frugal culture of subsidiary autonomy risks bureaucracy, as the chief executive of SDI has warned, and permanently higher central cost. A second impairment at Fire Testing Technology or Scientifica (about a 25% chance over 18 months) would revive the “cockroach” narrative, in which one hidden problem signals more, about the acquisition engine just as that engine tries to restart.

What would change my view. Positively: a completed acquisition at 4x to 6x EBIT under Armitage’s deal team; a high-quality external CFO from a larger listed peer; or a visible turnaround at Fire Testing Technology in the FY26 results commentary. Negatively: a further senior departure, or another dividend increase with FY26 cover below 1.5x.

Consensus versus my view. The sell-side describes the transition fully and leans positive on the team’s calibre. I agree on calibre but put more weight on the link between the dividend and leverage, which acts as the brake on the acquisition flywheel: the dividend takes 70% to 78% of free cash flow through FY28, which delays the restart of acquisitions by about 12 months relative to a peer that pays no dividend, such as SDI. No broker models a restart of acquisitions; the model does, at half the historical speed.

Score: 48. The change programme is broad, well resourced and sensible for the next five years, but it brings modest near-term earnings, a CFO vacancy, a stalled acquisition engine and a dividend promise that pre-empts the cash needed to restart that engine.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

About 85% to 90% of revenue sits in protected niches whose margins recover with volume, and the cash engine is intact; the part that is narrowing is the acquisition engine that drove past outperformance.

Industry structure and moats. Within each individual niche, which is the level that matters, Judges’ industry structure is excellent. About 20 of the 25 businesses are number one or two in bounded markets (for example UHV Design, Oxford Cryosystems, Sircal, EWB, Geotek, Korvus and Thermal Hazard Technology). In these markets, shares move about 1% a year, rivals compete on specification rather than price, instruments run for decades, design-in with OEM customers and embedded software lock customers in, and gross margins exceed 50%. The hardest evidence of the moats is that prices held through a 21% collapse in revenue: the margin damage from FY25 to H1 2026 came from lost volume, not from discounting.

Where the fragilities sit. The fragilities lie upstream and downstream of the niches. Demand is concentrated on politically set research budgets. Chinese localisation and low-end copies erode the price-sensitive edge of the portfolio (Armfield and Fire Testing Technology). The scientific-instrument industry is consolidating towards software-enabled, commercially exposed platforms (Halma, Danaher, Waters) that Judges does not join, and the market for acquisitions is contested. R&D at 7% of revenue is below peers’ 8% to 13%, and under-investment in R&D is how the three weak businesses fell behind.

Scale. Judges is small, and its scale brings financing and diversification but not purchasing power. Judges’ revenue of £146m compares with Halma’s £2.6bn, Renishaw’s £816m and Oxford Instruments’ £423m. Judges’ scale provides financing (a £90m bank facility plus a £50m accordion, running to 2030), diversification and a central team, but not purchasing power, software or a global service network. Central costs of about £5m are a fixed overhead that weighs most heavily when volumes are low.

Financial profile. Judges’ financial profile is structurally above average, but its current output is weak. The structural strengths of an asset-light assembly model are listed in the comparison below. The current weaknesses are these: the adjusted operating margin fell from 25.6% in FY23 to 19.2% in FY25 and 8.6% in H1 2026; ROTIC is 12.9% against a 30% target; statutory EPS is a third of adjusted EPS, because amortisation of acquired intangibles runs at £12m to £14m a year and impairments recur; and working capital is 16% of sales against a 10% aspiration. Free cash flow on a full definition (after capitalised development costs and leases) is 75% to 80% of adjusted net income, and the dividend’s share of that free cash flow has roughly doubled.

Management: credible and unproven. Prestidge has relevant sector experience and has been decisive in small ways: the £2m cost action, guidance held, and H1 2026 delivered at the midpoint. He made a small share purchase at 4,335p, and the whole executive team bought more shares through the Share Incentive Plan at 3,608p in October 2026. On paper the team is of high calibre.

Culture: distinctive and aligned with shareholders. About 40% of the 822 staff are shareholders; executive pay is in the bottom quartile (the chief executive earned £289k in 2025, and bonuses are nil in weak years); there has been no dilutive equity issuance; the dividend has risen by at least 10% in each of 20 years; and the group pays disciplined prices for acquisitions (3x to 7x EBIT, against Halma’s 10x to 12x).

Governance: weaker than at FTSE peers, but improving. Only three of eight directors are independent, the founder chairs the Nomination Committee, and the share-option hurdle of 5% EPS growth is soft.

Strategy and ambition: proven but not bold. The strategy (buy cheaply, hold forever and recycle the cash) is proven and smart. It offers no answer to software and automation, no pruning of the portfolio, no buybacks, and a slow rebalancing away from academia. The ambitions of a 30% ROTIC, “durable double-digit returns” and subsidiaries doubling their EBIT are credible as statements of intent, not as near-term forecasts.

Inference. About 85% to 90% of revenue sits in genuinely protected niches whose margins recover with volume, and the cash engine is intact. The historical source of outperformance, the mechanical recycling of cash into acquisitions at 5x EBIT, is the layer that is narrowing. A business of this quality earns 18% to 20% margins and a 15% to 19% ROTIC at mid-cycle volumes, which is good but no longer top-tier.

So what. Assumptions about margin recovery can lean on the niche structure with confidence. The fair multiple cannot lean on the compounder narrative until the new team completes an acquisition.

Strongest counter-case. Jefferies observed that Judges’ decentralised model produced “operational blindness”, and the Companies House record corroborates the observation: Fire Testing Technology’s loss widened while its R&D was cut, and more than 30% of subsidiaries changed leaders in 2024 to 2025. If the three or four challenged businesses (10% to 15% of revenue) keep eroding and a fourth or fifth joins them, the group’s blended economics will drift towards those of an ordinary engineering holding company, for which 14x earnings is the right multiple.

What would change my view. Positively: disclosure of subsidiary-level repair, even if only qualitative, in March 2027; a CFO appointed from a quality peer; or evidence of real price increases in commercial channels. Negatively: a second hidden problem of the “cockroach” kind, or central cost growth beyond the £5.2m to £5.4m assumed.

Consensus versus my view. The house brokers’ view that the “model is intact and long-term drivers are unaffected” is a narrative, not evidence, and the independent record (Jefferies’ research to April 2026, and Companies House filings) is more mixed. I sit between the two: the niche moats and the cash generation are robust, but the compounding engine is narrower than its history suggests, and its restart is an open question.

Score: 55. Excellent niche structure, strong cash generation and tangible returns, an aligned culture and a credible new team, set against a narrowing acquisition moat, a weak recent record of execution at the edges of the portfolio, below-peer R&D and a disclosure model that leaves the subsidiaries a black box.

4Conservative guidance; proactivity in keeping expectations conservative; track record

Judges’ guidance is conservative in its inputs but demanding in its execution, and the new team’s incentives point to a low March 2027 guide that can be beaten from July 2027.

Evidence: the FY26 guidance. Judges set FY26 guidance in January 2026 at 200p to 250p of adjusted EPS, cut from a consensus of about 300p, on two conservative stated inputs: no US recovery and no coring expedition. Since then the company has anchored to “in line with market expectations” of about 200p, the bottom of the range. The market does not believe the range’s midpoint, 12% above consensus, because the year needs about 80% of its EPS in H2, against a historical 50% to 55%: H2 EPS of about 160p, against about 134p in H2 2025. There will be no FY27 guidance until 24 March 2027, and there is no medium-term framework beyond the 30% ROTIC ambition, which the company reaffirms but cannot reach in the window.

Evidence: the record. Judges’ record against start-of-year expectations is poor: expected EPS was cut by 19% in FY24, by 26% in FY25 and by 33% so far in FY26 (chart below). Each cut was prompt and honest, which makes management an “honest tracker” rather than a sandbagger, and each rebased figure was then delivered or nearly delivered: FY24 landed inside its range, FY25 came in 3% below it, and H1 2026 landed at the midpoint. The longer record (only five years in twenty without a record result; total shareholder return compounding at 25% a year) belongs to a different funding era. The new chief executive has held one guidance range, and the last formal upgrade came in FY23.

Inference. Judges’ guidance is conservative in its inputs and demanding in its execution. The new team’s incentives (a bonus based on budget EPS, and a soft option hurdle measured from a rebased floor) and the precedents of SDI and discoverIE, whose new teams reset guidance low, point to a conservative March 2027 range, plausibly 205p to 240p, whose top would sit near the model’s 234p. That is the shape of a “guide low, beat later” setup. The first opportunity for the company to report trading “ahead of expectations” is the July 2027 update, when H1 2027 is compared with H1 2026’s 21% revenue fall and EPS of 39p.

So what. My probabilities for the January, March and July 2027 events are on the timeline in the summary. In addition, I put the probability that the FY27 outturn beats the midpoint of the March 2027 guidance at about 60%. The dividend policy of increases of at least 10% a year holds with about 80% probability. In the other 20% of outcomes the dividend is held flat rather than cut, triggered by FY26 EPS below about 180p and flat FY27 EPS.

Strongest counter-case. For three consecutive years the argument that “consensus is conservative on margin” was wrong, because volume fell. In both of the last two years weighted to Q4, the company fell short of September’s expectations (by about £4m in November 2024, and by 6% in January 2026). Judges has demonstrated that it can convert its order book into revenue; it has not demonstrated that it can forecast that conversion. Guidance that holds at 200p while needing 80% of the year’s EPS in Q3 and Q4 is more a ceiling than a floor.

What would change my view. A January 2027 update that confirms “in line”, with full-year order intake within 2% of FY25 and an order book of 15 to 17 weeks, would remove most of the FY26 risk and make the March guidance a floor. A Q4 slip of more than about £5m would mean that the model’s FY27 lean above consensus should be removed, not merely reduced.

Consensus versus my view. Consensus sits at 199p to 206p, the bottom of the guidance range, and treats FY26 as a trough but not a beatable one; I agree, and lean 4% lower. For FY27, the house broker (Zeus) has already written out the upgrade case: revenue 5% above the £128m consensus would push EPS to the top of the brokers’ range. The market has not priced that upgrade.

Score: 44. The inputs to guidance are conservative and the new team is incentivised to guide low, but the execution hurdle for FY26 is high, there has been no upgrade since 2023, and the three-year record against expectations is among the worst in the sector.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope and feedback loops

Operating leverage is the strongest feature of the case: each £1 of revenue regained returns 40p to 45p of operating profit, about twice the 18p to 24p in consensus, while pricing and cost-out add nothing net.

Operating leverage: the dominant mechanism. Operating leverage drives Judges’ earnings more than any other factor. Of a cost base of about £118m in FY25, raw materials (£44.8m, 31% of revenue) are variable and a further 3% to 5% of revenue is semi-variable. Staff costs (£48.5m), other external charges (£19.0m) and depreciation (£4.7m) form the fixed block: about £67m in FY25 and about £63m annualised in H1 2026, after cost actions and the disappearance of volume-linked pay. Gross contribution on marginal revenue is about 65%, so a 10% change in revenue (£12.5m) moves EBIT by about £8m, or 43% of FY26 EBIT, before any cost response. That is the widest range of earnings outcomes in the dashboard’s peer set.

The record shows the leverage working in both directions. From FY23 to H1 2026 Judges lost £16m of EBIT on £11m of lost revenue, a decremental margin of about 65% that was inflated by the loss of coring revenue at 65% to 75% margins. In 2015, and again from 2021 to 2023, the group rebuilt its margins on volume without price increases leading.

The realised incremental margin on recovery is 40% to 45%, about twice consensus’s 18% to 24%. The realised figure is lower than the 65% gross contribution because about £1m of semi-variable cost returns and because wage inflation (about £2.8m a year) is netted against price increases (about £3.3m a year). Broker sensitivity tables, at 4.2p of EPS per point of organic revenue growth, imply a drop-through of 25% to 30% and understate the mechanism; the model’s figure is about 9.6p per point.

Pricing power: defensive only. Judges’ prices recover cost inflation but add nothing to margin. About 85% of the businesses pass cost increases through, in 90% to 95% of cases, and no discounting was reported in the downturn. However, price realisation lagged inflation in FY25 (costing 170 basis points of margin); academic buyers defer purchases rather than negotiate, and increasingly resist price rises (in a Jefferies survey, 75% of US laboratory managers described conditions as weak); and the company has never quantified a price contribution. Price adds about 2.5% a year to revenue and nothing to margin. Real pricing power exists only in OEM-embedded vacuum products and commercial channels (perhaps a third of revenue), where it is worth at most 0.5 to 1 point of margin over the window, offset by negative real pricing in education, fire testing and China.

Financial leverage: a constraint, not an amplifier. Interest costs of £3.2m fall to £2.7m over the forecast period. The reference rate, SONIA (the Sterling Overnight Index Average), is swapped at 3.2% to 3.7% until 2028, so the live sensitivity is the lending-margin grid of 1.85% to 3.5%, worth about 4p of EPS between leverage of 2.0x and 1.5x. A 10% move in EBIT becomes an 11% to 12% move in profit before tax. The real effect of the debt is on the order in which cash is used: the dividend first, deleveraging second and acquisitions third.

Cost-out: small and early. Planned cost savings total about £2.8m by FY28 (£1.0m, £1.3m and £0.5m a year), 2% of the cost base, and inflation of £2.5m to £3m a year more than offsets the savings. A Renishaw-style programme (£23m of savings and 7% of headcount) is not available without abandoning decentralisation. The real internal lever is repairing the three loss-making or under-earning businesses, which together lose perhaps £1.5m to £2.5m of EBIT on £15m to £20m of revenue. Bringing those three businesses to a 10% margin would add 25p to 35p of EPS; the model credits half.

Feedback loops: the flywheel is held still by the brake. One powerful reinforcing loop (cash conversion funds acquisitions at 5x EBIT, which raise EPS and cash) is held still by one powerful balancing loop (earnings down, leverage up, dividend cover down, acquisitions paused). The operating-leverage loop (orders up, margin up, cash up, leverage down) releases the brake from FY28, and the acquisition flywheel restarts at about half speed. A negative loop at the weak businesses (lost market share, lost margin, R&D cut) is being countered by the centre. A latent balancing loop, in which de-rating removes the shares as an acquisition currency and makes a buyback competitive with deals, is ignored by the board.

Inference and so what. Revenue growth produces outsized profit growth at Judges, more than at any peer: organic EPS compounds at about 16% a year from FY26 to FY28 on organic revenue growth of about 6%. Judges is a one-lever model. Price and cost-out contribute nothing net, so the whole margin recovery comes from volume, and the whole volume story is the conversion of orders into revenue.

Strongest counter-case. The same operating leverage makes the downside steep: a revenue shortfall of 5% against the model in FY27 is about £4m of EBIT and 45p of EPS. The acquisition flywheel’s historical speed (1.3 deals a year, adding about 10 to 12 points of revenue growth) is also out of reach inside the window, because entry multiples are drifting up (5.5x assumed, against 5.3x historically) and the dividend leaves only £3m to £5m a year of retained cash.

What would change my view. An H1 2027 EBIT margin of 14% or better on about £63m of revenue, the model’s marker, would confirm the incremental margin; a margin below 12% would show that costs are being rebuilt. A share buyback announced under a new CFO would signal a change in capital-allocation philosophy, add about 1.5% to EPS for each £5m spent, and reset the narrative.

Consensus versus my view. The brokers’ words describe “very high incremental margins”, but their models use 18% to 24%; I use 40% to 45%. On pricing and cost-out I agree with consensus that neither contributes anything. On the acquisition flywheel, no broker models a restart; I do, at half the historical speed and identified separately.

Score: 62. Exceptional operating leverage from a trough on a half-fixed cost base is the single strongest feature of the case, held back by pricing that only recovers costs, negligible scope for cost-out and an acquisition loop that is stalled until FY28.

6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth and margins than the past

EPS compounds at about 20% a year from FY26 to FY30 (about 14% on organic earnings alone), but the recovery takes Judges back towards its past, not beyond it.

Phasing of the next 18 months. The next three half-years swing sharply, which is why the July and September 2027 updates will look much stronger than the January 2028 update. H2 2026 must deliver 80% of FY26 EPS on revenue down 8%, against an H2 2025 that had no coring revenue. H1 2027 EPS should be about 2.4 times H1 2026’s 39p, on revenue up 13% and a margin of 13.7%. H2 2027 revenue growth slows to about 4% against a comparison period weighted to Q4.

Scope for double-digit growth. EPS compounds at about 20% a year from FY26 to FY30 (about 14% on organic earnings alone), including +22% in FY27 and +21% in FY28 before any coring and with only £5m of acquisitions. That rate is high by any European standard, but it starts from a trough: FY28 EPS of 282p is 3% above FY25 and 25% below FY23, and organic EPS regains FY25’s level only in FY29.

Higher growth or margins than in the past? No: Judges will grow more slowly and earn lower margins than in its past. Revenue growth of about 11% a year (5% organic) is below the 19-year average of 19% (7% organic), because the acquisition leg runs at half speed. The operating margin recovers to 18% in FY28 and about 20% by FY30 without coring (21% in a coring year), against 22% to 27% in FY21 to FY23, because about £6m of structural cost added since FY23 lowers the attainable margin by about 4 points at any volume. ROTIC reaches about 15% in FY28 and 18% to 19% in FY29 to FY30, against the founder-era average of 29% and the 30% target.

Where the model differs from consensus, and why. The model’s revenue is 3% to 9% above consensus in every year, because of the gap between orders and revenue; the brokers’ segment forecasts themselves sum to £125m, not the £121m group median. Year by year:

  • FY26: EBIT 7% and EPS 4% below consensus, because consensus’s line items need an H2 margin that Judges’ cost structure cannot deliver.
  • FY27: EBIT 3% and EPS 7% above consensus, from the higher incremental margin, a 20% tax rate against Shore Capital’s 23%, and lower interest.
  • FY28: EBIT and EPS both 14% above consensus, about half from acquisitions and half from operating leverage.

FY26 EPS also carries about 5p to 7p of non-recurring Patent Box benefit (an 18% tax rate against a recurring 20% to 21%), so the recurring FY26 base is about 185p, and underlying FY27 EPS growth is nearer 26% than 22%.

Strongest counter-case. The out-years embed two capabilities the company has not yet shown (sourcing deals without the founder, and repairing three drifting businesses) and one event with only a one-in-three chance of falling in the named year (coring in FY29). The probability-weighted FY29 EPS is therefore nearer 340p than 393p, and the expected EPS growth path is about 16% a year, not the modal 20%. I have not changed the model’s inputs on this account. Placing one expedition in its single most probable year, and showing its contribution separately, is a defensible convention for a lumpy event with about an 80% chance of occurring inside the window, and the organic-only line gives Richard the alternative directly. The analysts’ change of the FY26 tax rate to 18% in their third research set also stands.

What would change the forecasts. Each dated event resolves part of the forecasts. The January 2027 update (Q4 conversion, full-year order intake and order-book weeks) resolves most of FY26 and a third of FY27. The March 2027 note on tax settles the recurring tax rate. The H1 2027 margin reported in July 2027 tests the incremental margin. A Geotek contract signature dates the 55p of coring EPS, and a first acquisition dates the restart of the flywheel.

Score: 58. EPS growth of about 20% a year for four years from a trough, with a realistic margin recovery to 18% to 20%, is strong in rate and well grounded in mechanics, but it is a recovery towards the past rather than beyond it, and about a quarter of the FY26 to FY28 uplift relies on capabilities not yet proven.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Estimate revisions should trace a shallow U, slightly negative to March 2027 and positive from July 2027, and the best-founded upgrade is to FY28 EBIT.

Evidence: consensus is low and internally inconsistent. Consensus FY26 and FY27 EPS has been cut 33% in twelve months and now sits at the bottom of the company’s own guidance range. Consensus excludes coring and acquisitions, embeds incremental margins of 18% to 24% and, at Shore Capital, a 23% tax rate against a guided 18% and a recurring 20% to 21%. The brokers’ line items are internally inconsistent: £121m of revenue with £20.3m of EBIT requires a 24% H2 margin, and the segment forecasts sum to £125m. One-month revisions are zero, the first month without a cut after a year of cuts. Investec’s FY27 forecast of 243p is 11% above the median and will move first in either direction.

Evidence: coverage is thin. FactSet’s set holds three brokers: two corporate brokers that publish no ratings, and Investec at Buy. Jefferies dropped coverage at Underperform in April 2026, and Berenberg (Buy, 5,600p target) sits outside FactSet’s set. Price targets of 6,450p to 7,200p are 90% to 110% above the share price and have a record of being cut while estimates hold.

The expected sequence of revisions, event by event.

EventExpected effect on consensus
22 January 2027FY26 EPS cut (35% probability), held (50%) or raised (15%). Even after a “met” update, brokers will nudge FY26 EBIT down and hold EPS through a lower tax rate, so revision data will record a negative EBIT revision.
24 March 2027The range of FY27 forecasts compresses towards the midpoint of the company’s guidance (Investec down; Shore Capital up, especially on tax); the median roughly holds.
July 2027If H1 2027 revenue grows about 10% or more at a margin above 13%, brokers raise FY27 EPS by 3% to 7% (to 225p to 235p) and FY28 by a similar amount, and the breadth of revisions turns positive for the first time since early 2023.
Over 18 monthsFY27 consensus (219p) ends higher with 50% probability, lower with 30% and within 2% with 20%: about 225p probability-weighted. FY28 consensus (248p) ends higher with 55% probability.
BeyondFY28 and FY29 consensus is more likely to be upgraded than cut (60% upgraded, 25% cut, 15% unchanged), because consensus contains none of the three things that the company’s history says will appear: operating leverage, acquisitions and coring. A fourth broker, or Jefferies’ return, is plausible after September 2027.

Inference. The 6-to-12-month window straddles the shallow U. The best-founded upgrade is to FY28 EBIT: £23.8m in consensus against £27.0m achievable, about half of the gap organic. The narrative can move from “casualty” to “recovery” within 6 to 12 months if the January update is clean, but it will not return to “compounder” until an acquisition completes and ROTIC visibly rises.

So what. There are two entry points, depending on the holder. For a holder who wants upgrade momentum before buying, the entry is after a clean 22 January 2027 update, or after 24 March 2027 if the company issues a conservative guide whose top sits near 234p. For a holder who wants to be early against the price, the entry is now, accepting a one-in-three chance of a 15% to 25% drawdown first.

Strongest counter-case. The three brokers are corporate brokers whose models already sit at the optimistic end of what the company tells them. The “latent upgrade” argument assumes that the brokers will adopt operating leverage they have so far refused to model, and the same argument has failed in each of the last three years. If NIH outlays (−15% in the latest quarter) are a better lead indicator than Judges’ own order intake, FY27 orders will stall in H2 2027 and the July “ahead of expectations” statement will never arrive.

What would change my view. Negative FY27 revisions after March 2027 beyond the expected compression of Investec’s forecast; an H1 2027 margin below 12%; or a US appropriations outcome that enacts funding cuts.

Consensus versus my view. Consensus describes a company that has stopped compounding and must reinvest its recovery; I describe a fixed-cost business recovering at half its old pace. The gap between the two views is favourable for FY27 and FY28, and, unusually, it lies in arithmetic that the brokers already acknowledge in words.

Score: 58. The conditions for upgrades are largely in place, and the mechanics of a July 2027 upgrade are arithmetic rather than hope, but the first event in the window leans towards a small cut, and coverage is too thin and too dominated by house brokers to carry a new narrative on its own.

8Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative, share price technicals, and peers

Momentum is negative on every measure; for an early entry that is the point, because the first positive momentum reading will arrive only after the multiple has started to move.

Evidence. Every measure of momentum at Judges is negative or flat:

Peers: the sector is split, and Judges is on the wrong side. Renishaw (technical momentum A, earnings momentum A, share price +44% over twelve months, Q1 revenue +47%), Jenoptik (D and A, +104%) and Vaisala (B and B, +43%) ride semiconductor, data-centre and defence capital spending that Judges barely touches. Halma (F and B, −3%) de-rated on its Avo acquisition despite raising its margin guidance. Tomra (F and F, −21%) is the only peer de-rating alongside Judges, for its own reasons. Judges’ true demand peers (Bruker, the academic side of Oxford Instruments, and SDI) are not in the dashboard’s peer basket. Bruker’s book-to-bill is above 1.0 for the fourth consecutive quarter and Oxford Instruments’ orders are up 44%, which indicates that the academic bottom is already in for better-positioned companies.

Inference. Momentum is negative-to-flat on every dimension at Judges and positive at its semiconductor-exposed peers, which is the signature of a stock at the bottom of its own cycle rather than of a sector at the bottom of its cycle. The only stabilising signs are the zero one-month revision and the share price holding above its 52-week low after the September results.

So what. The shares have no momentum support, and for Richard’s process that is the point: this case is “early and against the price”. The first positive momentum reading (a clean January update, with estimates flat to up) will be the entry signal for momentum-sensitive holders, and by then the multiple will already be moving.

Strongest counter-case. Negative momentum at a thinly traded AIM stock, with institutional sellers (Odin and Liontrust) and no new institutional buyers, can persist for quarters whatever the fundamentals. A liquidity event among UK small-caps could take the price to 3,000p without any company news.

What would change my view. The price reclaiming the 50-day average (about 3,800p) on strong volume after the January update; a positive one-month revision; or a new institutional holder crossing 3%.

Consensus versus my view. There is no disagreement about the facts: everyone can see that momentum is negative. The difference lies in what the negative momentum means. I read it as the late stage of a collapse rather than as a structural decline.

Score: 15. Momentum is negative on guidance, estimates, narrative and technicals, with the strong peers on the other side of a split sector; the only comfort is that revisions stopped falling this month.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple and its fragilities are few and named, but the range of outcomes is the widest in the peer set, and the first risk is binary and cannot be observed before 22 January 2027.

Simplicity. The case is unusually simple to state, because a few drivers explain almost all of the change in earnings:

1 driver
for the next 18 months: the conversion of recovered order intake into shipments, concentrated in Q4 2026 and H1 2027 and, within H1 2027, in a £4m to £6m China refill and the weak comparison with H1 2026
2 drivers
for the next four years: organic volume on a fixed cost base (54% of the change in EBIT from FY26 to FY28) and the restart of acquisitions (24%)
1 binary event
at any time: a single coring contract with a single state customer, worth about 55p of EPS in whichever year the expedition sails

Price, materials costs, interest, share count and, once the March 2027 note is published, tax barely matter. Although the portfolio is diffuse (25 businesses, thousands of customers and negligible bad debt), the drivers of change are concentrated: two-thirds of revenue follows public research budgets that move together.

Fragilities. Seven fragilities could break the case, and the first of them is binary and cannot be observed before 22 January 2027. The figure ranks them.

The range of outcomes. The distribution of outcomes is skewed down against FY26 consensus, roughly symmetric around the model’s base case, and skewed up against FY27 and FY28 consensus and the multiple, because the downside cases are mostly about timing while the upside cases are about the level of earnings.

Suddenness and trackability. Judges’ risks resolve suddenly, at four dated reporting events a year, and cannot be tracked between them. The company publishes no subsidiary data, no progress on Q4 shipments, no pipeline detail and no currency sensitivity, and its order-book weeks include orders whose delivery customers have asked to defer. External monitors partly fill the gap: monthly NIH outlays, Bruker (early November and February), Oxford Instruments (November), JEOL (November), SDI (December), Fugro and the sterling exchange rate.

Materiality and prevalence. Each risk event matters a great deal to the share price: the shares fell 20% after an update that held guidance, and at about $1m traded a day a few holders set the price. Such events are also frequent: three guidance changes in three years, two slips of the coring expedition and one dropped broker.

Precedents from Judges and its sector. High-fixed-cost makers are best bought at the turn, and volume-led recoveries from this kind of setup are usually delivered within two years. Judges’ own 2014 to 2016 recovery took the order book from 7.8 to 14.7 weeks and the margin to 17.3% within a year; its 2020 to 2022 recovery took the margin from about 19% to 28%, helped by counter-cyclical acquisitions. Renishaw lifted its margin from 15.7% to 18.7% within a year in 2025 to 2026, with EPS forecasts up 15% in a quarter, and Oxford Instruments recovered similarly in 2015 to 2017. Against these precedents, serial acquirers with drifting returns de-rate durably (Judges’ P/E fell from 35x to 14.5x as ROTIC fell from 23% to 13%), turnarounds take two to three years with a base rate of success of about 30%, and the Sector Digest’s own test for Judges is the January 2027 update.

Sentiment risks. The sentiment risks are external to Judges: a high discount rate (a 10-year yield of 5.1%, and the dashboard’s fragility tilt at Double Underweight); read-across from a profit warning at any academic-exposed peer or from a weak NIH print; a de-rating of compounders generally; US budget headlines; a single bearish initiation in a three-broker name; and the CFO’s departure feeding the narrative that Judges is a black box.

Consensus versus my view. The driver-dispersion research calls the outcomes “negatively skewed due to valuation risks”; I agree for the next trading update and disagree for the stock. The market also treats 2.1x as Judges’ leverage, when 2.1x is the seasonal June high.

Score: 35. The case is simple and its fragilities are few and named, but the range of outcomes is the widest in the peer set, the first risk is binary and unobservable, nobody models sterling, and the share’s own history says that a year weighted to Q4 is the kind of year it misses.

10Where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle

The stock is in the late stage of its collapse and shading into bottoming; a clean 22 January 2027 update would move it to turning up.

Evidence. The dashboard’s rule-based phase is “collapsing”, but the evidence for “bottoming” is now as strong, and only the evidence for “turning up” is missing.

Evidence for “collapsing”

  • Price −40.5% over twelve months, with the 200-day average falling in every one of them
  • EPS estimates −33% in twelve months
  • A broker dropped coverage
  • Institutional sellers
  • Multiple at the 0th percentile of five years
  • Dividend covered 1.1x at the interim
  • The CFO leaving

Evidence for “bottoming”

  • Orders turned in Q3 (−18%, flat, then about +15%)
  • The order book is level with a year ago
  • Estimates have stopped falling (0% over one month)
  • Guidance has held for nine months after being rebased on conservative inputs
  • The multiple is at the floor of its ten-year range (10th percentile 15.1x; now 14.7x on consensus)
  • Capitulation signatures: coverage dropped at Underperform, long-term institutions trimming, retail investors accumulating, no commentary at all
  • Management buying shares in small amounts
  • Academic-side peers (Bruker, Thermo Fisher, Oxford Instruments) reporting the bottom

Evidence against “turning up” yet

  • No reported revenue growth (H1 2026 −21%; H2 2026 will be −8%)
  • No upgrade
  • Price below every moving average
  • The Q4 test not yet passed

Inference. The stock is late in its collapse and shading into bottoming. The lifecycle moves to “turning up” on a clean 22 January 2027 update (a positive price reaction, with the multiple moving from 12x to 15x and then 17x), and the July 2027 update confirms the move with the first reported half of organic growth and the first “ahead of expectations” statement since 2023. “Thesis broadening” needs the second layer, a completed acquisition under the new team and a Geotek contract signature, plausibly in 2028; at that point the narrative can move from “recovery” to “compounder restarting” and the multiple towards its median. “Stalling” is the risk case: a January slip of more than about £5m together with a second leg of US funding cuts would hold the stock at 12x to 13x reduced earnings for another six to twelve months.

So what. Buying a bottoming stock before its trigger pays the most and risks the most. The asymmetry here favours being early: the downside of about 30% to 40% needs both an earnings miss and a de-rating, while the upside of about 50% needs only organic earnings and the guideline multiple. Being early should come with a position size that tolerates a 20% drawdown, or with the entry split across the January update.

Strongest counter-case. Bottoms in thinly covered AIM stocks can be long and flat. Judges spent 2016 to 2019 at 13x to 18x earnings as a smaller, less-known compounder. If the acquisition engine does not visibly restart, “bottoming” becomes “stalling” at a permanently lower multiple, and the recovery in EPS is capitalised at 14x rather than 17x.

What would change my view. A January slip, or an H1 2027 margin below 12%, would move my reading back to “collapsing” or “stalling”. A first acquisition and a coring contract signature in 2027 would move it to “turning up with the thesis broadening” a year early.

Consensus versus my view. The dashboard’s rule says “collapsing”, the house brokers say “trough” and the independent press says “struggling”. I say “bottoming, with a dated trigger”: a more constructive reading than the price action gives, and the same reading as the order book gives.

Score: 55. A bottoming stock whose turn is dated but unconfirmed is at an attractive point in its cycle, given this level of operating leverage, but the score is discounted for the real chance that the trigger disappoints first.

11The fair multiple

17x two-year-forward earnings is the right multiple for the next 6 to 18 months, applied to organic earnings only: about 5,000p at end-2027.

The guideline. The dashboard’s Phases page places the stock in “collapsing” by rule and sets the guideline fair multiple at 17.05x two-year-forward earnings, the 20th percentile of the stock’s own ten-year history (10th percentile 15.1x, median 21.6x, 75th percentile 26.2x, 90th percentile 31.1x). The guideline is 16% above the current 14.7x on consensus EPS and 39% above the current 12.3x on the model’s EPS.

My view: 17x is right for the next 6 to 18 months, for three reasons.

  1. The multiple is driven by the company, so the anchor is Judges’ own history. The R-squared of Judges’ returns against its peers is 0%, so peers’ multiples, such as Halma’s 23x or Renishaw’s 23x, are not the anchor.
  2. Judges’ history has two regimes, and the stock now belongs in the first. From 2016 to 2019, as a small, lightly covered compounder, Judges traded at 13x to 18x (averaging 14x to 15x). From 2019 to 2024, with ROTIC of 23% to 31% and frequent acquisitions, it traded at 20x to 35x. A stock turning up from a trough with its compounding engine stalled belongs in the upper half of the first regime, which is where 17x sits; it does not yet deserve the second regime.
  3. 17x is the midpoint while the compounder question is open. The analysts’ first research set framed 13x to 15x as fair for an organic-only, academically exposed niche manufacturer, which is where the stock trades now, and 18x to 22x as fair for a compounder with ROTIC heading to 18% to 20% and one or two acquisitions a year. The market is currently pricing the stalled case.

What would move the fair multiple. Down to 13x to 15x: a January slip and an FY27 cut, which would also lower the earnings to which the multiple applies (the trough scenarios of about 2,250p to 2,900p). Up to 20x to 22x, around the median: a completed acquisition at 4x to 6x EBIT in 2027, a Geotek contract signature, and ROTIC visibly rising through 15%. That upside is plausibly a 2028 story, worth about 4,900p to 6,400p on FY29 organic EPS of 292p.

On which earnings: organic, not layered. The model applies 17.05x to FY29 EPS of 393p at the end-2027 horizon. I would apply the multiple to organic FY29 EPS of 292p as the base case (about 4,980p) and treat the 101p from acquisitions and coring as options. A market pays a higher multiple for a restarted compounder; applying that multiple to earnings that already assume the restart would credit the restart before it has happened, and so count it twice. On this basis fair value at end-2027 is about 5,000p, rising to 5,800p to 6,700p if the two layers arrive. Even on today’s two-year-forward organic EPS of about 245p (a blend of FY27’s 229p and FY28’s 259p), 17x gives about 4,170p, 22% above the share price before any earnings growth.

Fair value at end-2027: about 5,000p on organic earnings at 17x, and 5,800p to 6,700p if acquisitions and coring arrive, against a share price of 3,425p.

Strongest counter-case. The ten-year percentile bands come from a period in which Judges was a premium compounder for seven of the ten years. A stock that has lost its compounding engine can trade below the 10th percentile of a history it no longer resembles, as Tomra does (4th percentile). The stock’s five-year low of 13.8x, rather than 17x, might be the right anchor until an acquisition is done.

What would change my view. Any of the three upside triggers (a completed acquisition, a coring contract signature or a rising ROTIC trend) would take my fair multiple to 20x. A CFO appointment that reopens buybacks would add a point. A second impairment would take the fair multiple down to 14x.

Consensus versus my view. House price targets of 6,500p to 7,200p imply about 28x to 30x FY27 consensus EPS: the old regime’s multiple applied to trough earnings. The targets have been cut 10% in three months and will be cut again before they are raised. I agree with the dashboard’s 17.05x as the multiple for a stock that is turning up, and I differ from the brokers by about 10 points of multiple.

Score: 68. A fair multiple 16% to 39% above the current one, anchored on the stock’s own history rather than on peers, with a clear path to the median if the compounding engine restarts, is a favourable position; the score is discounted for the real possibility that the history overstates what a stalled compounder deserves.

12Total shareholder return, split into earnings, multiple and dividends (the Dupont framework)

The return I would underwrite is about +52% to end-2027 on organic earnings; the model’s +102% needs both the acquisition and coring layers, and the probability-weighted return is about +30% to +35%.

The model’s return at the guideline multiple (share price 3,425p; 17.05x reached at the 18-month column).

Horizon Total return Annualised Value per share From earnings From the multiple From dividends
18-month column, to 31 December 2027 (14 months away) +102% +81% 6,924p +45.6% +34.3% +6.7%
Three-year column, to 30 June 2029 (32 months away) +113% +33% 7,304p +107.5% −2.6% +11.1%

How the two rows are built. The model’s horizons are its fixed columns, not 18 and 36 months from today, so the annualised figures are flattered. The first row applies 17.05x to the two-year-forward EPS at end-2027, which is FY29’s 393p, giving 6,700p; adding 229p of dividends (the FY26 final dividend and the FY27 dividends) gives 6,924p. The second row applies the same multiple to the forward earnings at mid-2029 (about 406p, the model’s extrapolation beyond FY30) and adds 380p of cumulative dividends. The multiple contributes nothing further in the second row because the re-rating is complete in the first, so earnings carry the three-year figure.

What drives the first-row return, in order of importance.

  1. The re-rating. The move from 12.3x to 17.05x is worth about +39% on its own and is the whole of the first row’s contribution from the multiple. The re-rating is the market agreeing that the trough is in, which the 22 January and July 2027 updates decide.
  2. Earnings. Two-year-forward EPS rises from about 278p today (a blend of FY27’s 234p and FY28’s 282p) to 393p at end-2027, an increase of 41%. Within FY29’s 393p, the operating-leverage recovery contributes about 60p over FY27’s organic 229p (taking organic EPS to 292p), the acquisition layer about 46p and the FY29 coring expedition about 55p.
  3. Dividends. A 3.7% yield growing 10% a year adds about 7% in 14 months and 11% in 32 months.

The layered reading Richard should use. With the multiple held at 17.05x and dividends at 229p, the end-2027 return falls from +102% with both layers to +52% on organic earnings alone (the four combinations are in the table under Judgement 5), and to +36% on a consensus-style extrapolation with no operating leverage (FY29 EPS of 260p). With organic FY29 EPS held at 292p, the return is +91% at the 21.6x median multiple, +52% at 17.05x and +30% with no re-rating (14.5x). The downside cases are these:

Downside caseAssumptionsShare priceTotal return to end-2027
A modest missFY27 EPS about 200p; two-year-forward EPS about 230p at 13xabout 2,990p−6%, with dividends
The analysts’ trough scenariosFY26 EPS about 170p and FY27 EPS 185p to 190p, at 12x to 13x2,250p to 2,450p−30% to −35%
A trough valued on enterprise valueTrough earnings on an enterprise-value basisabout 2,100p−40%

Inference. The model’s headline +102% is the most likely outcome only if both layers arrive on time; the organic-only +52% is the figure I would underwrite. Even the organic figure rests on two things: an arithmetic one (booked orders ship onto a fixed cost base) and a judgement (the market pays the 20th percentile of the stock’s own multiple history for a confirmed turn). The three-year return adds little to the 18-month return because the model’s multiple stops moving after end-2027 and FY30 EPS is flat on FY29, as the coring year drops out. Excluding coring, FY30 EPS grows about 16% on FY29, so the three-year organic return is about +65% to +70%.

So what. The skew is favourable, and the events that resolve it are dated. Weighting one-third on a January slip (−20% to −30% at first, recovering partially through 2027), one-half on the organic path (+50%) and one-sixth on the layers arriving early (+75% to +100%) gives an expected return over 14 months of the order of +30% to +35%. Two events, the January and July 2027 updates, resolve most of the dispersion.

Strongest counter-case. The return is a re-rating story dressed as an earnings story. Without a re-rating, the organic path pays +30% over 14 months, which is good but not exceptional for the risk, and the multiple moves only on Judges’ own events, the first of which has a one-in-three chance of going wrong. The acquisition and coring layers, 101p of FY29 EPS, carry probabilities of only 55% to 60% and 35% respectively in their named years.

What would change my view. The same dated events that drive the rest of this memo would change my view. In addition, sterling above $1.40 for a year would remove 47p to 83p from any out-year EPS and about 15 to 25 percentage points from these returns.

Consensus versus my view. House targets imply +90% to +110%, using 28x to 30x trough earnings; the model reaches a similar return using 17x recovered earnings including both layers; I reach about +50% using 17x organic earnings. All three views share a direction but not a construction, and the construction determines what an investor is paying for.

Score: 70. A base-case return of about +50% to +100% in 14 months, with dividends and an organic floor near +30% even without a re-rating, set against a downside of −30% to −40% that needs a miss and a de-rating together, is an unusually favourable distribution; the score is not higher because half the headline return depends on unproven layers and the first event could go the wrong way.

13Summary conclusion

Judges Scientific is a case about arithmetic that the market has stopped doing. The order book has turned, revenue follows in about four months, and profit follows revenue at 40p to 45p in the pound. The case will be decided on 22 January 2027 and confirmed in July 2027.

The business. Judges is a collection of protected niche instrument makers with 65% contribution margins, high cash conversion and a cost base that is half fixed. It is run by a credible new team and carries a dividend promise and 1.5x to 1.7x leverage, which slow the business but do not stop it. Judges has just lived through the worst 18 months in its listed history, almost entirely for external and political reasons, and both its earnings (191p, 49% below peak) and its multiple (12x to 14.5x two-year-forward earnings, the floor of a decade) show the damage.

The mechanism the market has missed. Judges’ order book has already turned: FY26 order intake is flat against revenue down 14%, Q3 intake is up 15%, and the order book is level with a year ago. Consensus prices neither the returning revenue nor the operating leverage. The three brokers’ models carry incremental margins of 18% to 24% and, in the lowest forecast, a 23% tax rate against a guided 18%.

The shape of the next 18 months. The next trading update is a genuine risk: there is about a one-in-three chance that FY26 EPS lands at 165p to 185p, depending on a Q4 that the company cannot see ahead for investors. The four reports that follow are set up to beat expectations, with the first “ahead of expectations” statement since 2023 available in July 2027 against a weak H1 2026 comparison of 39p.

The two layers of out-year earnings. Organic EPS of 229p, 259p and 292p in FY27 to FY29 is the layer I underwrite. Acquisitions plus one coring expedition take FY29 EPS to 393p, and I treat those layers as dated options worth about 50 percentage points of return. At the 17x guideline multiple, the organic path returns about +50% in 14 months with dividends, the full model returns +102%, and the trough cases return −30% to −40%.

The constraints. The constraints are real, and they should temper the narrative rather than the position. The margin ceiling is about 20%, not 26%; the compounding engine restarts at half speed and only from FY28; sterling is an unmodelled swing of 47p to 83p of EPS; and the company’s disclosure leaves investors blind between four dated reporting events.

The practical conclusion. The case will be decided on 22 January 2027 and confirmed in July 2027. A handful of holders set the price of a stock that trades about $1m a day. Being early means accepting the risk of the first event in exchange for a re-rating that, on this share’s history, moves first and moves far.

End notes

  1. Bases and sources. Unless stated otherwise, profit figures are on the company’s adjusted basis, which is also the brokers’ basis. “The model” is the Financial Analyst’s model after update 2; figures labelled “Viewforth” in charts and tables are the model’s. “Consensus” is the FactSet median of three brokers (two for FY28). The share price is 3,425p at 22 October 2026 (3,450p on 21 October).
  2. Research references. “The dashboard” is the Viewforth stock dashboard, including its Phases page, peer set and ratings. “The analysts’ first research set” and “third research set” refer to successive packs of analysts’ work behind this memo; the third set changed the FY26 tax rate to 18%.
  3. Terms. ROTIC: return on total invested capital. NIH: the US National Institutes of Health. OEM: original equipment manufacturer. SONIA: the Sterling Overnight Index Average. AIM: the London Stock Exchange’s Alternative Investment Market. EBITA: earnings before interest, tax and amortisation. Incremental margin: the extra operating profit earned on each extra pound of revenue. Book-to-bill: orders received divided by revenue billed.
  4. The model’s history columns. The model summary’s FY23 to FY25 history columns are FactSet’s lines after amortisation (EPS of £2.07, £1.61 and £0.48), so the summary’s FY26 EPS growth of +298% is an artefact of the change of basis; on the adjusted basis, FY26 EPS growth is −31%.
  5. Net debt definitions. The model’s year-end net debt (£35.1m for FY26) sits about £6m below the analysts’ company-definition figure in every year, an opening-balance or definitional gap that does not affect EPS. The forecast table uses the company’s definition.
  6. Total shareholder return. The split of total shareholder return into earnings, multiple and dividends is the model template’s own.
  7. Charts. Charts drawn for this page take their figures from the memo. Colours: history and organic earnings in blue, consensus in violet, the model in orange, and falls and risks in red. The default financial tables and the trajectory chart show FactSet’s reported basis for history, which differs from the adjusted figures in the text (for example, FY25 EPS).
  8. Derived figures. The half-year table derives H2 2025 and H1 2026 revenue, H1 2026 EBIT, the H2 2027 margin and H2 2027 EPS from the full-year and half-year figures in the memo. The cost-structure bar splits FY25 revenue approximately, taking the semi-variable slice at about 4% of revenue.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 1.99, +314.2% against 0.48 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves -17.0%.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:
